claim: Centrosome loss had no effect on the ability of endothelial cells to polarize and move in 2D and 3D environments.
source: Here, we show that centrosome loss had no effect on the ability of endothelial cells to polarize and move in 2D and 3D environments.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Non-centrosomal microtubules stabilized by CAMSAP2 were required for directional migration on 2D substrates.
source: In contrast, non-centrosomal microtubules stabilized by the microtubule minus-end-binding protein CAMSAP2 were required for directional migration on 2D substrates and for the establishment of polarized cell morphology in soft 3D matrices.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Non-centrosomal microtubules stabilized by CAMSAP2 were required for the establishment of polarized cell morphology in soft 3D matrices.
source: In contrast, non-centrosomal microtubules stabilized by the microtubule minus-end-binding protein CAMSAP2 were required for directional migration on 2D substrates and for the establishment of polarized cell morphology in soft 3D matrices.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CAMSAP2 was important for persistent endothelial cell sprouting during in vivo zebrafish vessel development.
source: CAMSAP2 was also important for persistent endothelial cell sprouting during in vivo zebrafish vessel development.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data from zebrafish experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the absence of CAMSAP2, cell polarization in 3D could be partly rescued by centrosome depletion.
source: In the absence of CAMSAP2, cell polarization in 3D could be partly rescued by centrosome depletion, indicating that in these conditions the centrosome inhibited cell polarity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The centrosome inhibits cell polarity in the absence of CAMSAP2.
source: In the absence of CAMSAP2, cell polarization in 3D could be partly rescued by centrosome depletion, indicating that in these conditions the centrosome inhibited cell polarity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data stated in the abstract.

claim: CAMSAP2-protected non-centrosomal microtubules are needed for establishing cell asymmetry by enabling microtubule enrichment in a single-cell protrusion.
source: We propose that CAMSAP2-protected non-centrosomal microtubules are needed for establishing cell asymmetry by enabling microtubule enrichment in a single-cell protrusion.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The centrosome has been assumed to play a central role in governing cell polarity.
source: By analogy with the compass on a ship navigating to its destination, the centrosome has been assumed to play a central role in governing cell polarity (Bornens, 2012), including two-dimensional (2D) mesenchymal migration, in which cells are organized into an extending leading edge and a contractile cell rear (Ridley et al., 2003; Tang and Marshall, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: During migration, the centrosome is typically positioned at the front of the nucleus.
source: The widely accepted dogma connecting the centrosome and the direction of cell movement originated from the observation that during migration, the centrosome is typically positioned at the front of the nucleus (Gotlieb et al., 1981; Koonce et al., 1984; Kupfer et al., 1982; Malech et al., 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Centrosome positioning at the front of the nucleus is observed in different systems.
source: Such centrosome positioning is observed in different systems (Elric and Etienne-Manneville, 2014; Luxton and Gundersen, 2011), although it does not apply to certain specific cell types (Luxton and Gundersen, 2011; Yvon et al., 2002) or in the presence of environmental constraints (Doyle et al., 2009; Pouthas et al., 2008; Schütze et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Centrosome positioning at the front of the nucleus does not apply to certain specific cell types or in the presence of environmental constraints.
source: Such centrosome positioning is observed in different systems (Elric and Etienne-Manneville, 2014; Luxton and Gundersen, 2011), although it does not apply to certain specific cell types (Luxton and Gundersen, 2011; Yvon et al., 2002) or in the presence of environmental constraints (Doyle et al., 2009; Pouthas et al., 2008; Schütze et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The orientation of the nucleo-centrosomal axis is commonly regarded as a major cell polarity determinant.
source: Despite the scarcity of direct experimental evidence, currently based on laser ablation of the pericentrosomal area (Koonce et al., 1984; Wakida et al., 2010) or indirect interference with centrosome localization (Dujardin et al., 2003; Etienne-Manneville and Hall, 2001; Levy and Holzbaur, 2008; Schmoranzer et al., 2009), the orientation of the nucleo-centrosomal axis is commonly regarded as a major cell polarity determinant.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Microtubules are thought to support cell polarity by forming an asymmetrical network.
source: Microtubules (MTs) are thought to support cell polarity by forming an asymmetrical network (Etienne-Manneville, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: MT asymmetry can be generated by specific positioning of the centrosomal anchor of a radial MT network relative to other cell structures.
source: This asymmetry can potentially be generated by specific positioning of the centrosomal anchor of a radial MT network relative to other cell structures, such as the nucleus, but also by MTs that do not originate from the centrosome (Akhmanova and Hoogenraad, 2015; Alieva et al., 2015; Vinogradova et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MT asymmetry can be generated by MTs that do not originate from the centrosome.
source: This asymmetry can potentially be generated by specific positioning of the centrosomal anchor of a radial MT network relative to other cell structures, such as the nucleus, but also by MTs that do not originate from the centrosome (Akhmanova and Hoogenraad, 2015; Alieva et al., 2015; Vinogradova et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The minus ends of centrosome-independent MTs can associate with members of the CAMSAP/Patronin/Nezha family.
source: The minus ends of centrosome-independent MTs can associate with the members of the calmodulin-regulated spectrin-associated protein (CAMSAP)/Patronin/Nezha family (Akhmanova and Hoogenraad, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In mammalian cells, CAMSAP2, together with CAMSAP3 in certain cell types, binds to free, non-centrosomal MT minus ends and promotes their stabilization.
source: In mammalian cells, CAMSAP2, together with CAMSAP3 in certain cell types, binds to free, non-centrosomal MT minus ends and promotes their stabilization (Jiang et al., 2014; Tanaka et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CAMSAP2 has been shown to participate in MT stabilization at the Golgi apparatus.
source: Interestingly, CAMSAP2 has recently been shown to participate in MT stabilization at the Golgi apparatus (Wu et al., 2016), a site that can function as an alternative MT-organizing centre (MTOC) (Zhu and Kaverina, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Golgi apparatus can function as an alternative MT-organizing centre (MTOC).
source: Interestingly, CAMSAP2 has recently been shown to participate in MT stabilization at the Golgi apparatus (Wu et al., 2016), a site that can function as an alternative MT-organizing centre (MTOC) (Zhu and Kaverina, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In mammalian cells, the Golgi is often positioned close to the centrosome.
source: In mammalian cells, the Golgi is often positioned close to the centrosome (Rios, 2014), and thus locates in front of the nucleus during cell migration (Koonce et al., 1984; Kupfer et al., 1982; Malech et al., 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Golgi locates in front of the nucleus during cell migration.
source: In mammalian cells, the Golgi is often positioned close to the centrosome (Rios, 2014), and thus locates in front of the nucleus during cell migration (Koonce et al., 1984; Kupfer et al., 1982; Malech et al., 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: An anteriorly positioned Golgi is thought to support polarized transport needed to sustain directional migration.
source: As the central organizer of the secretory pathway, an anteriorly positioned Golgi is thought to support polarized transport needed to sustain directional migration (Yadav and Linstedt, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Golgi disorganization without MT disassembly prevents proper polarized Golgi trafficking without affecting global secretory properties but leads to defects in directional cell movement.
source: Consistently, Golgi disorganization without MT disassembly (Bisel et al., 2008; Hurtado et al., 2011; Yadav et al., 2009), as well as the loss of Golgi-associated MTs (Hurtado et al., 2011; Miller et al., 2009) prevent proper polarized Golgi trafficking without affecting global secretory properties but lead to defects in directional cell movement.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The loss of Golgi-associated MTs prevents proper polarized Golgi trafficking without affecting global secretory properties but leads to defects in directional cell movement.
source: Consistently, Golgi disorganization without MT disassembly (Bisel et al., 2008; Hurtado et al., 2011; Yadav et al., 2009), as well as the loss of Golgi-associated MTs (Hurtado et al., 2011; Miller et al., 2009) prevent proper polarized Golgi trafficking without affecting global secretory properties but lead to defects in directional cell movement.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Investigation of the contributions of centrosomal and Golgi-originating MT populations to Golgi organization indicated that the role of the centrosome was restricted to facilitating assembly of an integral Golgi apparatus.
source: Notably, investigation of the contributions of centrosomal and Golgi-originating MT populations to Golgi organization indicated that the role of the centrosome was restricted to facilitating assembly of an integral Golgi apparatus (Vinogradova et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: During angiogenesis, endothelial cells respond to external cues by coordinating numerous activities, including proliferation, sprouting, migration, lumen formation and anastomosis.
source: During angiogenesis, the process of new blood vessel development, endothelial cells (ECs) respond to external cues by coordinating numerous activities, including proliferation, sprouting, migration, lumen formation and anastomosis (Geudens and Gerhardt, 2011; Potente et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The first step of vessel formation, outward cell sprouting, requires that the tip cell breaks symmetry by extending protrusions toward guidance cues.
source: The first step of vessel formation, outward cell sprouting, requires that the tip cell, which will guide growth of a new vessel, breaks symmetry by extending protrusions toward guidance cues (Geudens and Gerhardt, 2011; Lee and Bautch, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MT growth dynamics has been shown to be required for the formation and maintenance of angiogenic structures.
source: MT growth dynamics has been shown to be required for the formation and maintenance of angiogenic structures (Bayless and Johnson, 2011; Myers et al., 2011), whereas its regional regulation has been implicated in directional EC migration (Braun et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Regional regulation of MT growth dynamics has been implicated in directional EC migration.
source: MT growth dynamics has been shown to be required for the formation and maintenance of angiogenic structures (Bayless and Johnson, 2011; Myers et al., 2011), whereas its regional regulation has been implicated in directional EC migration (Braun et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Vascular sprouting and repolarization are affected by supernumerary centrosomes, a hallmark of tumor ECs that impacts on MT nucleation and dynamics.
source: Vascular sprouting and repolarization are also affected by supernumerary centrosomes, a hallmark of tumor ECs that impacts on MT nucleation and dynamics (Kushner et al., 2014; Kushner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ECs respond to a monolayer wound by developing a mesenchymal motile phenotype typified by a front-rear asymmetry and anterior centrosome positioning.
source: The ability of ECs to polarize can be explored in 2D, where cells respond to a monolayer wound by developing a mesenchymal motile phenotype typified by a front-rear asymmetry and anterior centrosome positioning (Gotlieb et al., 1981).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: When cultured in 3D collagen gels, ECs form branched tubular structures.
source: When cultured in 3D collagen gels, ECs form branched tubular structures (Koh et al., 2008), and when spheroids of ECs are embedded in a 3D matrix, they develop sprouts that closely reproduce the first step of formation of capillaries from pre-existing vessels (Pfisterer and Korff, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: When spheroids of ECs are embedded in a 3D matrix, they develop sprouts that closely reproduce the first step of formation of capillaries from pre-existing vessels.
source: When cultured in 3D collagen gels, ECs form branched tubular structures (Koh et al., 2008), and when spheroids of ECs are embedded in a 3D matrix, they develop sprouts that closely reproduce the first step of formation of capillaries from pre-existing vessels (Pfisterer and Korff, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The centrosome and the Golgi apparatus are positioned anteriorly in migrating ECs in 2D.
source: Using 2D monolayer wound healing assay, we confirmed the anterior position of the centrosome and the Golgi apparatus in migrating ECs and also extended this observation to tip ECs sprouting from a spheroid in 3D (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The centrosome and the Golgi apparatus are positioned anteriorly in tip ECs sprouting from a spheroid in 3D.
source: Using 2D monolayer wound healing assay, we confirmed the anterior position of the centrosome and the Golgi apparatus in migrating ECs and also extended this observation to tip ECs sprouting from a spheroid in 3D (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Centrinone prevents centriole duplication and leads to centrosome depletion.
source: To assess the impact of centrosome removal on these processes, we took advantage of the Plk4 inhibitor centrinone, which prevents centriole duplication and leads to centrosome depletion (Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Efficient centrosome elimination was confirmed by staining with different markers of centrioles or pericentriolar material (PCM).
source: Efficient centrosome elimination was confirmed by staining with different markers of centrioles or pericentriolar material (PCM) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Loss of centrosomes as focal points of MT organization was visible by super-resolution imaging of the MT networks in fixed cells and by tracing growing EB3-GFP-positive MTs in live cells.
source: Loss of centrosomes as focal points of MT organization was also visible by super-resolution imaging of the MT networks in fixed cells and by tracing growing EB3-GFP-positive MTs in live cells (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: The centrosomal arrangement of MTs in control cells was more obvious in EB3-GFP tracings than in MT images.
source: Importantly, the centrosomal arrangement of MTs in control cells was more obvious in EB3-GFP tracings than in MT images (Figure 1A,B), suggesting that the centrosome plays a more important role in nucleating new MTs than in anchoring their minus ends, and that even in control cells, a significant MT population is non-centrosomal.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: The centrosome plays a more important role in nucleating new MTs than in anchoring their minus ends.
source: Importantly, the centrosomal arrangement of MTs in control cells was more obvious in EB3-GFP tracings than in MT images (Figure 1A,B), suggesting that the centrosome plays a more important role in nucleating new MTs than in anchoring their minus ends, and that even in control cells, a significant MT population is non-centrosomal.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Even in control cells, a significant MT population is non-centrosomal.
source: Importantly, the centrosomal arrangement of MTs in control cells was more obvious in EB3-GFP tracings than in MT images (Figure 1A,B), suggesting that the centrosome plays a more important role in nucleating new MTs than in anchoring their minus ends, and that even in control cells, a significant MT population is non-centrosomal.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: The perinuclear MT density was partly associated with the Golgi apparatus.
source: The perinuclear MT density was partly associated with the Golgi apparatus, which was mildly enlarged and less compact in centrinone-treated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The Golgi apparatus was mildly enlarged and less compact in centrinone-treated cells.
source: The perinuclear MT density was partly associated with the Golgi apparatus, which was mildly enlarged and less compact in centrinone-treated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Nocodazole washout assays showed that the centrosome was the major nucleation site during MT reassembly in control cells.
source: Nocodazole washout assays showed that the centrosome was the major nucleation site during MT reassembly in control cells, while this function was taken over by the Golgi membranes in centrinone-treated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: MT nucleation function was taken over by the Golgi membranes in centrinone-treated cells.
source: Nocodazole washout assays showed that the centrosome was the major nucleation site during MT reassembly in control cells, while this function was taken over by the Golgi membranes in centrinone-treated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: MT density was not affected by centrinone treatment.
source: In spite of these differences, MT density, the density of growing, EB3-positive MT plus ends, parameters of MT plus end growth and the levels of different tubulin post-translational modifications were not affected (Figure 1A,B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B), and in contrast to a centrosome excess (Godinho et al., 2014), the distribution and intensity of cell-cell adhesion markers was unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D ) ().
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The density of growing, EB3-positive MT plus ends was not affected by centrinone treatment.
source: In spite of these differences, MT density, the density of growing, EB3-positive MT plus ends, parameters of MT plus end growth and the levels of different tubulin post-translational modifications were not affected (Figure 1A,B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B), and in contrast to a centrosome excess (Godinho et al., 2014), the distribution and intensity of cell-cell adhesion markers was unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D ) ().
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Parameters of MT plus end growth were not affected by centrinone treatment.
source: In spite of these differences, MT density, the density of growing, EB3-positive MT plus ends, parameters of MT plus end growth and the levels of different tubulin post-translational modifications were not affected (Figure 1A,B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B), and in contrast to a centrosome excess (Godinho et al., 2014), the distribution and intensity of cell-cell adhesion markers was unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D ) ().
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The levels of different tubulin post-translational modifications were not affected by centrinone treatment.
source: In spite of these differences, MT density, the density of growing, EB3-positive MT plus ends, parameters of MT plus end growth and the levels of different tubulin post-translational modifications were not affected (Figure 1A,B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B), and in contrast to a centrosome excess (Godinho et al., 2014), the distribution and intensity of cell-cell adhesion markers was unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D ) ().
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: In contrast to a centrosome excess, the distribution and intensity of cell-cell adhesion markers was unchanged after centrinone treatment.
source: In spite of these differences, MT density, the density of growing, EB3-positive MT plus ends, parameters of MT plus end growth and the levels of different tubulin post-translational modifications were not affected (Figure 1A,B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B), and in contrast to a centrosome excess (Godinho et al., 2014), the distribution and intensity of cell-cell adhesion markers was unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D ) ().
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and a citation to previous literature.

claim: The abundance of MT minus-end stabilizing protein CAMSAP2 was mildly but not significantly increased after centrinone treatment.
source: The abundance of MT minus-end stabilizing protein CAMSAP2 was mildly but not significantly increased, and the area occupied by CAMSAP2 stretches was enlarged (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,C.

claim: The area occupied by CAMSAP2 stretches was enlarged after centrinone treatment.
source: The abundance of MT minus-end stabilizing protein CAMSAP2 was mildly but not significantly increased, and the area occupied by CAMSAP2 stretches was enlarged (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,C.

claim: The enlarged area occupied by CAMSAP2 stretches is consistent with the enlarged Golgi, to which many CAMSAP2 stretches attach.
source: This is consistent with the enlarged Golgi, to which many CAMSAP2 stretches attach (Wu et al., 2016), and possibly with an increased stabilization of non-centrosomal MTs that compensate for the loss of the centrosomal ones.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and a citation to previous literature.

claim: The enlarged area occupied by CAMSAP2 stretches is possibly due to an increased stabilization of non-centrosomal MTs that compensate for the loss of the centrosomal ones.
source: This is consistent with the enlarged Golgi, to which many CAMSAP2 stretches attach (Wu et al., 2016), and possibly with an increased stabilization of non-centrosomal MTs that compensate for the loss of the centrosomal ones.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on experimental data.

claim: 2D migration was not perturbed in centrinone-treated ECs.
source: 2D migration was not perturbed in centrinone-treated ECs (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: ECs in the migrating front showed proper polarized organization with their Golgi positioned toward the direction of migration after centrinone treatment.
source: ECs in the migrating front still showed proper polarized organization with their Golgi positioned toward the direction of migration (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Centrosome removal did not affect the emergence of EC sprouts out of spheroids grown in collagen matrix.
source: In a more physiological 3D context, centrosome removal did not affect the emergence of EC sprouts out of spheroids grown in collagen matrix (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The few remaining centrosome-containing ECs were not enriched in the sprouts after centrinone treatment.
source: The few remaining centrosome-containing ECs were not enriched in the sprouts, and the Golgi apparatus was properly polarized in sprouting tip ECs devoid of centrosomes (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The Golgi apparatus was properly polarized in sprouting tip ECs devoid of centrosomes.
source: The few remaining centrosome-containing ECs were not enriched in the sprouts, and the Golgi apparatus was properly polarized in sprouting tip ECs devoid of centrosomes (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: CPAP is a factor essential for centriole duplication.
source: To confirm these results, we depleted centrosomes by knocking down CPAP, a factor essential for centriole duplication (Kohlmaier et al., 2009; Schmidt et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CPAP knockdown efficiently removed centrosomes in the majority of cells without affecting EC polarization in 3D and sprouting from spheroids.
source: Also using this approach, we could efficiently remove centrosomes in the majority of cells without affecting EC polarization in 3D and sprouting from spheroids (Figure 1G,H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2F,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G,H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2F,G.

claim: The centrosome is dispensable for endothelial polarization and movement.
source: These results indicate that centrosome is dispensable for endothelial polarization and movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CAMSAP2 expression was transiently enhanced upon treatment with the angiogenic factor VEGF.
source: Interestingly, CAMSAP2 expression was transiently enhanced upon treatment with the angiogenic factor VEGF, and the length and number of CAMSAP2-decorated MT stretches was increased (Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that non-centrosomal MTs might play a role in angiogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The length and number of CAMSAP2-decorated MT stretches was increased upon treatment with VEGF.
source: Interestingly, CAMSAP2 expression was transiently enhanced upon treatment with the angiogenic factor VEGF, and the length and number of CAMSAP2-decorated MT stretches was increased (Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that non-centrosomal MTs might play a role in angiogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Non-centrosomal MTs might play a role in angiogenesis.
source: Interestingly, CAMSAP2 expression was transiently enhanced upon treatment with the angiogenic factor VEGF, and the length and number of CAMSAP2-decorated MT stretches was increased (Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that non-centrosomal MTs might play a role in angiogenesis.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CAMSAP2 silencing generated a mostly centrosome-anchored, radial MT array.
source: To test this idea, we silenced CAMSAP2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), thereby generating a mostly centrosome-anchored, radial MT array (Figure 2C,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CAMSAP2 silencing had no effect on the MT density.
source: This treatment had no effect on the MT density or parameters of MT plus end dynamics (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CAMSAP2 silencing had no effect on parameters of MT plus end dynamics.
source: This treatment had no effect on the MT density or parameters of MT plus end dynamics (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The abundance of post-translationally modified forms of tubulin was unchanged after CAMSAP2 silencing.
source: The abundance of post-translationally modified forms of tubulin was also unchanged (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), showing that ECs are in this respect different from U2OS cells, where loss of detyrosinated MTs was seen upon CAMSAP2 depletion (Jiang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and a citation to previous literature.

claim: ECs are different from U2OS cells, where loss of detyrosinated MTs was seen upon CAMSAP2 depletion.
source: The abundance of post-translationally modified forms of tubulin was also unchanged (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), showing that ECs are in this respect different from U2OS cells, where loss of detyrosinated MTs was seen upon CAMSAP2 depletion (Jiang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and a citation to previous literature.

claim: MT nucleation from the centrosome was unaffected by CAMSAP2 silencing.
source: MT nucleation from the centrosome was unaffected, in line with fact that CAMSAP2 shows no colocalization with the centrosome (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: CAMSAP2 shows no colocalization with the centrosome.
source: MT nucleation from the centrosome was unaffected, in line with fact that CAMSAP2 shows no colocalization with the centrosome (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: The motility of the motor protein kinesin-3 KIF13B was unchanged after CAMSAP2 silencing.
source: Since MT properties were largely unaltered, the motility of the motor protein kinesin-3 KIF13B, which is known to play an important role in transporting VEGF receptor in ECs (Yamada et al., 2014), was also unchanged (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H and a citation to previous literature.

claim: KIF13B is known to play an important role in transporting VEGF receptor in ECs.
source: Since MT properties were largely unaltered, the motility of the motor protein kinesin-3 KIF13B, which is known to play an important role in transporting VEGF receptor in ECs (Yamada et al., 2014), was also unchanged (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: CAMSAP2 depletion caused a moderate but significant decrease in cell migration in 2D.
source: CAMSAP2 depletion caused a moderate but significant decrease in cell migration in 2D (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1I.

claim: The defect in cell migration was much more pronounced during 3D sprouting after CAMSAP2 depletion.
source: Strikingly, the defect was much more pronounced during 3D sprouting: ECs depleted of CAMSAP2 were able to form only shorts sprouts and form long protruding structures (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: ECs depleted of CAMSAP2 were able to form only short sprouts and not long protruding structures.
source: Strikingly, the defect was much more pronounced during 3D sprouting: ECs depleted of CAMSAP2 were able to form only shorts sprouts and form long protruding structures (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: The strong impairment in 3D sprouting after CAMSAP2 depletion was not related to cell viability or cell cycle progression defects.
source: This strong impairment was not related to cell viability or cell cycle progression defects (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), and CAMSAP2 depletion in non-cycling ECs still severely affected formation of long sprouts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: CAMSAP2 depletion in non-cycling ECs still severely affected formation of long sprouts.
source: This strong impairment was not related to cell viability or cell cycle progression defects (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), and CAMSAP2 depletion in non-cycling ECs still severely affected formation of long sprouts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).

claim: Rescue experiments using expression of a siRNA-insensitive CAMSAP2 construct confirmed the specificity of the phenotype.
source: Rescue experiments using expression of a siRNA-insensitive CAMSAP2 construct confirmed the specificity of the phenotype (Figure 2H), with ECs positive for the rescue construct populating growing sprouts in a CAMSAP2 knockdown background (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H,I.

claim: ECs positive for the rescue construct populated growing sprouts in a CAMSAP2 knockdown background.
source: Rescue experiments using expression of a siRNA-insensitive CAMSAP2 construct confirmed the specificity of the phenotype (Figure 2H), with ECs positive for the rescue construct populating growing sprouts in a CAMSAP2 knockdown background (Figure 2I).

claim: CAMSAP3 was only weakly expressed in ECs.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–E.

claim: CAMSAP3 depletion did not aggravate the phenotype of CAMSAP2 knockdown.
source: We also analyzed the potential involvement of CAMSAP3 and found that it was only weakly expressed in ECs and its depletion did not aggravate the phenotype of CAMSAP2 knockdown (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–E.

claim: CAMSAP2 has an important and specific role in EC morphology in 3D.
source: These data point to an important and specific role of CAMSAP2 in EC morphology in 3D.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Early stages of sprout formation were not affected much by CAMSAP2 depletion.
source: We found that early stages of sprout formation were not affected much by CAMSAP2 depletion; however, the differences gradually increased over time, as, in contrast to the control situation, spheroids silenced for CAMSAP2 were unable to increase the number and especially the length of the sprouts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Spheroids silenced for CAMSAP2 were unable to increase the number and especially the length of the sprouts over time.
source: We found that early stages of sprout formation were not affected much by CAMSAP2 depletion; however, the differences gradually increased over time, as, in contrast to the control situation, spheroids silenced for CAMSAP2 were unable to increase the number and especially the length of the sprouts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the absence of CAMSAP2, endothelial spheroids are capable of initiating protrusions but are unable to mature them into larger and more stable, MT-populated structures.
source: In the absence of CAMSAP2, endothelial spheroids are thus capable of initiating protrusions but are unable to mature them into larger and more stable, MT-populated structures (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CAMSAP2 depletion did not prevent the establishment of a vascular plexus when individual isolated ECs were cultured in a collagen matrix.
source: In line with this idea, when individual isolated ECs were cultured in a collagen matrix, where they extended protrusions in different directions and fused into a tubulogenic network, CAMSAP2 depletion did not prevent the establishment of a vascular plexus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Protrusive activity of isolated ECs measured by their elongation and the total and average protrusion length was not affected by CAMSAP2 knockdown.
source: Protrusive activity of isolated ECs measured by their elongation (inverse of circularity) and the total and average protrusion length was not affected by CAMSAP2 knockdown (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CAMSAP2-depleted ECs bearing a centrosome-centered MT array had a different organization of protrusions.
source: However, such CAMSAP2-depleted ECs bearing a centrosome-centered MT array (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) had a different organization of protrusions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Control ECs had a restricted number of protrusions, with a single predominant one.
source: Whereas control ECs had a restricted number of protrusions, with a single predominant one, CAMSAP2-depleted ECs displayed multiple short protrusions (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: CAMSAP2-depleted ECs displayed multiple short protrusions.
source: Whereas control ECs had a restricted number of protrusions, with a single predominant one, CAMSAP2-depleted ECs displayed multiple short protrusions (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Control ECs had most of their protrusions, and especially the longest ones, aligned in one direction.
source: In contrast to control ECs that had most of their protrusions, and especially the longest ones, aligned in one direction, CAMSAP2-depleted cells displayed protrusions that were more radially dispersed, irrespective of their length (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: CAMSAP2-depleted cells displayed protrusions that were more radially dispersed, irrespective of their length.
source: In contrast to control ECs that had most of their protrusions, and especially the longest ones, aligned in one direction, CAMSAP2-depleted cells displayed protrusions that were more radially dispersed, irrespective of their length (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Control ECs, after having formed several small transient protrusions, stabilized and extended one or two of them.
source: To understand the origin of this phenotype, we performed live recording of protrusion formation. In contrast to control ECs, which, after having formed several small transient protrusions, stabilized and extended one or two of them, CAMSAP2-depleted ECs were unable to accomplish this transition and to elongate in a single direction (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: CAMSAP2-depleted ECs were unable to stabilize and extend protrusions and to elongate in a single direction.
source: To understand the origin of this phenotype, we performed live recording of protrusion formation. In contrast to control ECs, which, after having formed several small transient protrusions, stabilized and extended one or two of them, CAMSAP2-depleted ECs were unable to accomplish this transition and to elongate in a single direction (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Quantification of protrusion dynamics pointed to dramatically lower protrusion persistence after CAMSAP2 inactivation.
source: Quantification of protrusion dynamics using a radial reslice representation (Figure 3F; every black signal represents the presence of a protrusion at a given time point at a given radial position) confirmed these observations and pointed to dramatically lower protrusion persistence after CAMSAP2 inactivation (Figure 3F), while the total protrusion number was not affected by CAMSAP2 depletion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The total protrusion number was not affected by CAMSAP2 depletion.
source: Quantification of protrusion dynamics using a radial reslice representation (Figure 3F; every black signal represents the presence of a protrusion at a given time point at a given radial position) confirmed these observations and pointed to dramatically lower protrusion persistence after CAMSAP2 inactivation (Figure 3F), while the total protrusion number was not affected by CAMSAP2 depletion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: In CAMSAP2-depleted cells with a radial MT array, MTs cannot become enriched in one protrusion.
source: We hypothesized that in CAMSAP2-depleted cells with a radial MT array, MTs cannot become enriched in one protrusion, and found that this indeed was the case (Figure 3G), strongly suggesting that non-centrosomal MTs stabilize polarized elongated cell morphology by enabling MT enrichment in a single protrusion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Non-centrosomal MTs stabilize polarized elongated cell morphology by enabling MT enrichment in a single protrusion.
source: We hypothesized that in CAMSAP2-depleted cells with a radial MT array, MTs cannot become enriched in one protrusion, and found that this indeed was the case (Figure 3G), strongly suggesting that non-centrosomal MTs stabilize polarized elongated cell morphology by enabling MT enrichment in a single protrusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: In 2D-cultured CAMSAP2-depleted cells, a modest increase in the density of F-actin cytoskeleton was observed.
source: In 2D-cultured CAMSAP2-depleted cells, we observed a modest increase in the density of F-actin cytoskeleton (Figure 4A), due to the presence of more stress fibers (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The modest increase in the density of F-actin cytoskeleton in 2D-cultured CAMSAP2-depleted cells was due to the presence of more stress fibers.
source: In 2D-cultured CAMSAP2-depleted cells, we observed a modest increase in the density of F-actin cytoskeleton (Figure 4A), due to the presence of more stress fibers (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CAMSAP2-depleted cells established normal polarized front-rear morphologies in 2D.
source: Beside this small difference, cells established normal polarized front-rear morphologies, as revealed by the presence of actin-enriched lamellipodia and myosin IIb-positive retracting cell edges, and the distribution patterns of active Rho and Rac1, as well as cell adhesion markers were normal (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B,C.

claim: The distribution patterns of active Rho and Rac1 were normal in CAMSAP2-depleted cells in 2D.
source: Beside this small difference, cells established normal polarized front-rear morphologies, as revealed by the presence of actin-enriched lamellipodia and myosin IIb-positive retracting cell edges, and the distribution patterns of active Rho and Rac1, as well as cell adhesion markers were normal (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B,C.

claim: Cell adhesion markers were normal in CAMSAP2-depleted cells in 2D.
source: Beside this small difference, cells established normal polarized front-rear morphologies, as revealed by the presence of actin-enriched lamellipodia and myosin IIb-positive retracting cell edges, and the distribution patterns of active Rho and Rac1, as well as cell adhesion markers were normal (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B,C.

claim: Actin cytoskeleton was unchanged in 3D environment in the absence of CAMSAP2.
source: Importantly, actin cytoskeleton was unchanged in 3D environment in the absence of CAMSAP2, displaying intense peripheral cortical accumulation as in control situation (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Myosin II-dependent cell contractility has been shown to inhibit protrusion formation in ECs.
source: Myosin II-dependent cell contractility has been shown to inhibit protrusion formation in ECs (Fischer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Inhibition of myosin II led to longer 3D protrusions in each condition.
source: In agreement with these observations, inhibition of myosin II either directly, with blebbistatin, or indirectly, with the inhibitor of the kinase ROCK (Y-27632), led to longer 3D protrusions in each condition (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: In the absence of CAMSAP2, myosin II inhibition did not rescue the polarized elongated morphology typical of control ECs.
source: However, in the absence of CAMSAP2, these treatments did not rescue the polarized elongated morphology typical of control ECs (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,C,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,C,E.

claim: Although decreased contractility facilitated protrusion persistence, CAMSAP2 depletion still severely reduced protrusion stability in the presence of the ROCK inhibitor.
source: Moreover, although decreased contractility facilitated protrusion persistence, CAMSAP2 depletion still severely reduced protrusion stability in the presence of the ROCK inhibitor (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Treatment of spheroids with the ROCK inhibitor or blebbistatin induced more and longer sprouts but failed to rescue sprouting impairment in CAMSAP2-depleted cells.
source: Similarly, treatment of spheroids with the ROCK inhibitor or blebbistatin induced more and longer sprouts but failed to rescue sprouting impairment in CAMSAP2-depleted cells (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Changes in acto-myosin cytoskeleton or contractility cannot explain the defects associated with CAMSAP2 silencing.
source: Altogether, these data demonstrate that changes in acto-myosin cytoskeleton or contractility cannot explain the defects associated with CAMSAP2 silencing.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CAMSAP2-depleted cells were often unable to orient their lamellae in the direction of migration.
source: While displaying normal front-rear morphologies, CAMSAP2-depleted cells were often unable to orient their lamellae in the direction of migration, suggesting polarity defects (Figure 4B, asterisks).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CAMSAP2 inactivation resulted in a substantial drop in the directionality of cell movement.
source: Accordingly, CAMSAP2 inactivation resulted in a substantial drop in the directionality of cell movement (Figure 5A), which was associated with Golgi and centrosome mispositioning respective to the wound (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CAMSAP2 inactivation was associated with Golgi and centrosome mispositioning respective to the wound.
source: Accordingly, CAMSAP2 inactivation resulted in a substantial drop in the directionality of cell movement (Figure 5A), which was associated with Golgi and centrosome mispositioning respective to the wound (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The Golgi and the centrosome always colocalized.
source: Furthermore, the correlation between the positions of the Golgi and the centrosome, which always colocalized (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), and the lamellipodia was strongly diminished after CAMSAP2 silencing, with some ECs having their leading edge in front of the Golgi and some not (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The correlation between the positions of the Golgi and the centrosome and the lamellipodia was strongly diminished after CAMSAP2 silencing.
source: Furthermore, the correlation between the positions of the Golgi and the centrosome, which always colocalized (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), and the lamellipodia was strongly diminished after CAMSAP2 silencing, with some ECs having their leading edge in front of the Golgi and some not (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Forward-targeted post-Golgi vesicle trafficking was perturbed in the absence of CAMSAP2.
source: Forward-targeted post-Golgi vesicle trafficking, which is often considered as a key regulator of cell polarity during migration, was perturbed in the absence of CAMSAP2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In control ECs the majority of exocytotic vesicles labeled with Rab6 moved towards the leading edge.
source: Whereas in control ECs the majority of exocytotic vesicles labeled with the small GTPase Rab6 moved towards the leading edge, Rab6 trajectories were distributed more symmetrically in CAMSAP2-depleted ECs, while the other trafficking parameters were not affected (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Rab6 trajectories were distributed more symmetrically in CAMSAP2-depleted ECs.
source: Whereas in control ECs the majority of exocytotic vesicles labeled with the small GTPase Rab6 moved towards the leading edge, Rab6 trajectories were distributed more symmetrically in CAMSAP2-depleted ECs, while the other trafficking parameters were not affected (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Other trafficking parameters were not affected in CAMSAP2-depleted ECs.
source: Whereas in control ECs the majority of exocytotic vesicles labeled with the small GTPase Rab6 moved towards the leading edge, Rab6 trajectories were distributed more symmetrically in CAMSAP2-depleted ECs, while the other trafficking parameters were not affected (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The symmetric distribution of Rab6 trajectories in CAMSAP2-depleted ECs likely reflected a more radial, symmetric MT array in these cells.
source: This likely reflected a more radial, symmetric MT array in these cells (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Golgi positioning does not directly dictate the orientation of the extending lamellae but is needed to stabilize directional persistence by controlling polarized trafficking.
source: Together, our 2D results argue in favor of a model where Golgi positioning does not directly dictate the orientation of the extending lamellae but is needed to stabilize directional persistence by controlling polarized trafficking.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Forward positioning of the Golgi was even more striking in 3D.
source: Forward positioning of the Golgi, which strongly co-localized with CAMSAP2 stretches, was even more striking in 3D (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The Golgi strongly co-localized with CAMSAP2 stretches.
source: Forward positioning of the Golgi, which strongly co-localized with CAMSAP2 stretches, was even more striking in 3D (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CAMSAP2 proved to be essential for Golgi polarization in the direction of sprouting in 3D.
source: In this 3D setting, CAMSAP2 proved to be essential for Golgi polarization in the direction of sprouting (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Control cells displayed highly asymmetric trafficking of MT-dependent Rab6 positive exocytotic vesicles in 3D.
source: In line with our 2D observations, while control cells displayed highly asymmetric trafficking of MT-dependent Rab6 positive exocytotic vesicles, little asymmetry in trafficking was observed between protrusions of CAMSAP2-depleted cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Little asymmetry in trafficking was observed between protrusions of CAMSAP2-depleted cells in 3D.
source: In line with our 2D observations, while control cells displayed highly asymmetric trafficking of MT-dependent Rab6 positive exocytotic vesicles, little asymmetry in trafficking was observed between protrusions of CAMSAP2-depleted cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Centrosome-anchored MTs cannot redistribute to a single protrusion.
source: Consistent with the inability of centrosome-anchored MTs to redistribute to a single protrusion (Figure 3G), the failure in polarization of the secretory trafficking, which is likely necessary to generate a stable leading cell edge (Schmoranzer et al., 2003; Stehbens et al., 2014; Yadav et al., 2009) could explain the inability of CAMSAP2 depleted ECs to form mature sprouts in 3D.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The failure in polarization of the secretory trafficking is likely necessary to generate a stable leading cell edge.
source: Consistent with the inability of centrosome-anchored MTs to redistribute to a single protrusion (Figure 3G), the failure in polarization of the secretory trafficking, which is likely necessary to generate a stable leading cell edge (Schmoranzer et al., 2003; Stehbens et al., 2014; Yadav et al., 2009) could explain the inability of CAMSAP2 depleted ECs to form mature sprouts in 3D.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The failure in polarization of the secretory trafficking could explain the inability of CAMSAP2 depleted ECs to form mature sprouts in 3D.
source: Consistent with the inability of centrosome-anchored MTs to redistribute to a single protrusion (Figure 3G), the failure in polarization of the secretory trafficking, which is likely necessary to generate a stable leading cell edge (Schmoranzer et al., 2003; Stehbens et al., 2014; Yadav et al., 2009) could explain the inability of CAMSAP2 depleted ECs to form mature sprouts in 3D.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and citations to previous literature.

claim: Two proteins, AKAP450 and myomegalin (MMG), are needed for anchoring CAMSAP2-decorated MT minus-ends to Golgi membranes.
source: To test this idea, we made use of our recent findings showing that two proteins, AKAP450 and myomegalin (MMG), are needed for anchoring CAMSAP2-decorated MT minus-ends to Golgi membranes (Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Depletion of AKAP450 or MMG displaced CAMSAP2 stretches from the Golgi.
source: As expected, depletion of AKAP450 or MMG (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) displaced CAMSAP2 stretches from the Golgi (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Depletion of AKAP450 or MMG had remarkably similar consequences for 2D migration compared to CAMSAP2 silencing.
source: This redistribution had remarkably similar consequences for 2D migration compared to CAMSAP2 silencing: ECs that had lost their Golgi-attached CAMSAP2 were unable to maintain directionality and to orient their Golgi, resulting in migration deficiency (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: ECs that had lost their Golgi-attached CAMSAP2 were unable to maintain directionality and to orient their Golgi, resulting in migration deficiency.
source: This redistribution had remarkably similar consequences for 2D migration compared to CAMSAP2 silencing: ECs that had lost their Golgi-attached CAMSAP2 were unable to maintain directionality and to orient their Golgi, resulting in migration deficiency (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Displacing non-centrosomal CAMSAP2-bound MT ends from Golgi by depleting AKAP450 or MMG had a negative impact on endothelial sprouting abilities.
source: Interestingly, the situation differed when ECs were placed in a 3D context: whereas displacing non-centrosomal CAMSAP2-bound MT ends from Golgi by depleting AKAP450 or MMG had a negative impact on endothelial sprouting abilities, its effect was significantly milder than that of CAMSAP2 depletion, when most MTs were attached to the centrosome (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The effect of displacing non-centrosomal CAMSAP2-bound MT ends from Golgi was significantly milder than that of CAMSAP2 depletion in 3D sprouting.
source: Interestingly, the situation differed when ECs were placed in a 3D context: whereas displacing non-centrosomal CAMSAP2-bound MT ends from Golgi by depleting AKAP450 or MMG had a negative impact on endothelial sprouting abilities, its effect was significantly milder than that of CAMSAP2 depletion, when most MTs were attached to the centrosome (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In 3D sprouting, non-centrosomal MTs might have a role independent of their direct Golgi association.
source: This suggests that in 3D sprouting, non-centrosomal MTs might have a role independent of their direct Golgi association.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on experimental data.

claim: Non-centrosomal MTs can redistribute more easily to create asymmetry.
source: We reasoned that non-centrosomal MTs, which are not anchored to a single point, might redistribute more easily to create asymmetry, and therefore, centrosome removal in CAMSAP2-depleted ECs might improve their polarization potential by restoring a pool of non-centrosomal MTs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on reasoning.

claim: Centrosome removal in CAMSAP2-depleted ECs might improve their polarization potential by restoring a pool of non-centrosomal MTs.
source: We reasoned that non-centrosomal MTs, which are not anchored to a single point, might redistribute more easily to create asymmetry, and therefore, centrosome removal in CAMSAP2-depleted ECs might improve their polarization potential by restoring a pool of non-centrosomal MTs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on reasoning.

claim: ECs silenced for AKAP450, MMG and CAMSAP2 in combination with centrinone-induced centrosome depletion were viable and efficiently lost their centrosome.
source: To test this idea, we silenced AKAP450, MMG and CAMSAP2 in ECs in combination with centrinone-induced centrosome depletion. Such ECs were viable and efficiently lost their centrosome, displaying a characteristic enlarged shape filled with a dense non-centrosomal MT array, even in the absence of CAMSAP2 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: ECs silenced for AKAP450, MMG and CAMSAP2 in combination with centrinone-induced centrosome depletion displayed a characteristic enlarged shape filled with a dense non-centrosomal MT array, even in the absence of CAMSAP2.
source: To test this idea, we silenced AKAP450, MMG and CAMSAP2 in ECs in combination with centrinone-induced centrosome depletion. Such ECs were viable and efficiently lost their centrosome, displaying a characteristic enlarged shape filled with a dense non-centrosomal MT array, even in the absence of CAMSAP2 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The density of MTs and growing, EB3-positive MT ends was similar in all conditions after centrosome depletion.
source: The density of MTs and growing, EB3-positive MT ends was similar in all conditions (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Acentrosomal cells showed enhanced recruitment of γ-tubulin to the Golgi.
source: As we described in our previous study (Wu et al., 2016), acentrosomal cells showed enhanced recruitment of γ-tubulin to the Golgi, an effect that was abolished by depleting AKAP450 (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C,D and a citation to previous literature.

claim: Enhanced recruitment of γ-tubulin to the Golgi in acentrosomal cells was abolished by depleting AKAP450.
source: As we described in our previous study (Wu et al., 2016), acentrosomal cells showed enhanced recruitment of γ-tubulin to the Golgi, an effect that was abolished by depleting AKAP450 (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C,D and a citation to previous literature.

claim: Abundant MT nucleation from the Golgi membranes was observed after nocodazole washout in control, MMG- and CAMSAP2-depleted acentrosomal cells.
source: In line with these results, we observed abundant MT nucleation from the Golgi membranes after nocodazole washout in control, MMG- and CAMSAP2-depleted acentrosomal cells, while in AKAP450-depleted acentrosomal cells, MTs were nucleated from the cytoplasmic sites distinct from the Golgi membranes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In AKAP450-depleted acentrosomal cells, MTs were nucleated from the cytoplasmic sites distinct from the Golgi membranes.
source: In line with these results, we observed abundant MT nucleation from the Golgi membranes after nocodazole washout in control, MMG- and CAMSAP2-depleted acentrosomal cells, while in AKAP450-depleted acentrosomal cells, MTs were nucleated from the cytoplasmic sites distinct from the Golgi membranes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The distribution of MT nucleation sites correlated with the recruitment of the pericentriolar material (PCM) marker Pericentrin to the Golgi in control, MMG- and CAMSAP2-depleted centrinone-treated cells.
source: Such distribution of MT nucleation sites correlated with the recruitment of the pericentriolar material (PCM) marker Pericentrin to the Golgi in control, MMG- and CAMSAP2-depleted centrinone-treated cells, and its dispersion in the cytoplasm in AKAP450-depleted cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Pericentrin was dispersed in the cytoplasm in AKAP450-depleted cells.
source: Such distribution of MT nucleation sites correlated with the recruitment of the pericentriolar material (PCM) marker Pericentrin to the Golgi in control, MMG- and CAMSAP2-depleted centrinone-treated cells, and its dispersion in the cytoplasm in AKAP450-depleted cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: MT density was detached from the Golgi region after AKAP450 and MMG knockdown.
source: In agreement with our previous work in RPE1 cells (Wu et al., 2016), MT density was detached from the Golgi region after AKAP450 and MMG knockdown, because these proteins constitute a part of an essential link between MTs and the Golgi membranes (Figure 7A,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A,D and a citation to previous literature.

claim: AKAP450 and MMG constitute a part of an essential link between MTs and the Golgi membranes.
source: In agreement with our previous work in RPE1 cells (Wu et al., 2016), MT density was detached from the Golgi region after AKAP450 and MMG knockdown, because these proteins constitute a part of an essential link between MTs and the Golgi membranes (Figure 7A,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A,D and a citation to previous literature.

claim: In CAMSAP2-depleted ECs, centrinone treatment caused some disorganization of the Golgi.
source: In CAMSAP2-depleted ECs, centrinone treatment caused some disorganization of the Golgi, and MTs were not concentrated in the Golgi area either (Figure 7A,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A,D.

claim: MTs were not concentrated in the Golgi area in CAMSAP2-depleted ECs after centrinone treatment.
